points.t: Any patient presenting with ‘cellulitis’, especially if both legs are involved, it is chronic or itchy, or there is no fever.
Most bilateral red legs are venous (stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis) or oedema, not infection.
Ask: one leg or two, acute or chronic, fever or not, itch or pain? Treat the actual cause.
Necrotising fasciitis, sepsis, DVT, critical ischaemia and diabetic foot infection.

points: Ask: **one leg or two?** Acute or chronic? Fever or rigors? Itch or pain? Is there a portal of entry?
Mark the border and record observations (NEWS2).
Wells score with D-dimer or Doppler if DVT is possible.
Check pulses or ABPI if there is an ulcer, or before compression.

cards.name: Venous eczema / stasis dermatitis
cards.clue: Bilateral or chronic, itchy, scale, haemosiderin, no fever

cards.name: Acute lipodermatosclerosis
cards.clue: Painful, woody, red skin above the ankle, often misdiagnosed as cellulitis

cards.name: DVT
cards.clue: Calf pain and swelling, less intense redness

cards.name: Contact dermatitis (e.g. to dressings)
cards.clue: Itchy, vesicular, matches the area covered

cards.name: Necrotising fasciitis
cards.clue: **Severe pain out of proportion**, rapid progression, systemic toxicity. **ED**

cards.name: Pyoderma gangrenosum / vasculitis
cards.clue: Ulcer edge features, purpura, systemic disease

items.t: Pain out of proportion, purple bullae, crepitus, or a rapidly spreading area: **necrotising fasciitis**.
Sepsis signs: low blood pressure, tachycardia, confusion, mottling.
A cold, pulseless or ischaemic limb.
A diabetic foot that is hot, red or ulcerated.

pearls.t: Venous eczema responds to emollient plus a topical steroid and compression (after ABPI). Antibiotics do nothing for it.
Recurrent ‘cellulitis’ in the same leg may be lipodermatosclerosis. Look at the whole leg history.
